title: Short Stuff: Unspent Campaign Money
summary: Short Stuff episode on what happens to unspent campaign money when a candidate drops out or loses. The hosts explain the difference between candidate campaign accounts and super PACs, FEC rules barring personal use of leftover funds, permissible uses such as donating to a party or charity or transferring to a super PAC, and how debt and loans are handled. They use Jeb Bush (about $152 million raised in the 2016 cycle), Rick Perry (super PAC money returned to billionaire donors), and Scott Walker (about $1 million in debt when he dropped out in September 2015) as examples, and note that campaign committees persist into a second term.

segments.title: Introduction and the Jeb Bush question
segments.summary: Josh introduces the topic of unspent campaign money, prompted by a How Stuff Works article. He and Chuck discuss whether donors wonder where their contributions go, and use Jeb Bush's 2016 campaign, which raised about $152 million yet did not win the nomination, as the example of leftover funds.

segments.title: Candidate funds versus super PACs
segments.summary: The hosts explain the two main sources of campaign money: the candidate's own campaign and super PACs, which after Citizens United can raise and spend unlimited funds so long as they do not coordinate with the candidate. They discuss how candidates typically spend contributions quickly, and what cash on hand means.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: Short break before returning to FEC rules.

segments.title: FEC rules on personal use and permissible uses
segments.summary: The main FEC rule is that leftover funds cannot be used for personal expenses. Permissible uses include donating to a party, to a charity, or to another candidate, with a $2,000 limit on personal donations to another candidate. Transfers to a super PAC are described as allowed, though the hosts say they are not fully certain of the details.

segments.title: Super PAC refunds and Rick Perry; debt and Scott Walker
segments.summary: Super PAC money is usually backed by a few wealthy donors who get it back if the candidate exits early. Rick Perry's super PAC, funded by billionaires in Dallas, had about $13 million unspent when he left, while his campaign raised only around $1 to $1.5 million. Scott Walker left the race in September 2015 with about $1 million in debt. Candidates who are wealthy can repay debts, while others may carry personal loans.

segments.title: Loan write-offs and campaigns that persist
segments.summary: Loans to a campaign over $250 are written off as donations after a set period following the election. Campaign committees continue as ongoing entities, so funds can be kept for a second-term run, as with Donald Trump's first term.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Josh closes the episode and promotes HowStuffWorks.
